title: Advanced Clause Analysis
description: Master advanced clauses for Grade 11: noun clauses in every position, reduced relative clauses, cleft sentences and nominal relative clauses — bilingual notes, practice and tests.

topics.title: Noun Clauses — Every Position
topics.concept:
A noun clause does any job a noun can do. Learn to spot it in each position:

  • Subject: What she said surprised us.
  • Object of a verb: I know that she is right.
  • Complement (after 'be'): The truth is that he failed.
  • Object of a preposition: I am sure of what he said.
  • After an adjective: I am afraid that he might fail.
  • In apposition to a noun: The fact that he lied is shocking.

Noun clauses begin with that, what, whether, if, who, why, how, where. After a preposition or as a subject, the clause itself is the 'noun'.

examples.problem: Identify the noun clause and its role: Whether he comes depends on the weather.
examples.solution: 'Whether he comes' — the subject of the verb 'depends' (a noun clause).

examples.problem: Identify the noun clause: I was not aware of how serious it was.
examples.solution: 'how serious it was' — object of the preposition 'of'.

recap: A noun clause does any job a noun can (subject/object/complement)
It can follow a preposition or an adjective

topics.title: Reduced Relative Clauses & Nominal Relatives
topics.concept:
Reduced relative clauses tighten a relative clause into a phrase:

  • Active → present participle: The woman who is standing there → The woman standing there.
  • Passive → past participle: The book which was written by him → The book written by him.
  • Sometimes → infinitive: He was the first who arrived → He was the first to arrive.

Cleft sentences split a sentence for emphasis (covered fully in a later chapter): It was Ram who broke the window.

Nominal relative clauses combine a noun + a relative pronoun into one word (whoever, whatever, whichever, what, where):

  • Whoever works hard succeeds. (= the person who works hard)
  • Give it to whoever asks. / I'll do what is needed.

examples.problem: Reduce the relative clause: The boy who was selected for the team is my cousin.
examples.solution: The boy selected for the team is my cousin. — passive → past participle.

examples.problem: Identify the nominal relative clause: Whoever finishes first wins.
examples.solution: 'Whoever finishes first' — it acts as the subject (= the person who finishes first).

recap: Reduce active relatives to '-ing'; passive to '-ed' participles
Some reduce to an infinitive (the first to arrive)
Nominal relatives (whoever, what) = noun + relative in one

questions.explanation: 'The reason is that …' — a noun clause, not 'because'.

outcomes: Identify noun clauses in subject, object and complement positions
Use noun clauses after prepositions and adjectives
Reduce relative clauses to participle or infinitive phrases
Analyse complex sentences into their clauses

intro.en: At this level, clause analysis becomes a precision tool. You will see noun clauses doing every job a noun can do, learn to reduce long relative clauses into tight phrases, and meet the nominal relative clause ('Whoever works hard succeeds'). These structures are the building blocks of mature, academic writing.
intro.hi: इस स्तर पर clause analysis एक सटीक उपकरण बन जाता है। आप noun clauses को वह हर काम करते देखेंगे जो संज्ञा कर सकती है, लंबे relative clauses को कसे हुए वाक्यांशों में reduce करना सीखेंगे, और nominal relative clause से मिलेंगे ('Whoever works hard succeeds')। ये संरचनाएँ परिपक्व, शैक्षणिक लेखन की आधारशिला हैं।

real_life.situation:
An academic sentence packs several clauses:

Sentence: What the report revealed surprised everyone, although the woman standing there already knew that the data were flawed.
real_life.why: 'What the report revealed' is a noun clause (subject); 'the woman standing there' is a reduced relative clause; 'that the data were flawed' is a noun clause (object). Recognising each makes a dense sentence instantly clear — and lets you write like this yourself.

quick_test.q: In 'What he wants is unclear', the underlined clause is the:
quick_test.explanation: 'What he wants' is the subject of 'is' — a noun clause.

common_mistakes.wrong: I know that what he said.
common_mistakes.note: Don't stack 'that' and 'what'; one connector is enough.

common_mistakes.wrong: The man who standing there is my uncle.
common_mistakes.right: The man standing there is my uncle.

common_mistakes.wrong: I am sure that what he means.
common_mistakes.right: I am sure of what he means.
common_mistakes.note: A noun clause after an adjective may need a preposition ('sure of').
No comma after a nominal-relative subject.

reading.passage: What the committee decided shocked the staff. The plan, proposed by the new director, would cut jobs. Whoever questioned it was ignored. "The fact that no one was consulted is the real problem," said an officer standing at the back. In the end, what mattered was not the policy itself but how it had been forced upon them.

questions.q: Identify the noun clause that is the subject of the first sentence.
questions.answer: 'What the committee decided' — the subject of 'shocked'.

questions.q: Find a reduced relative clause and restore its full form.
questions.answer: 'proposed by the new director' = 'which was proposed by the new director'; 'standing at the back' = 'who was standing at the back'.

questions.q: Identify the nominal relative clause.
questions.answer: 'Whoever questioned it' — the subject (= the person who questioned it).

speaking: I am sure of what I saw.
The man standing there is the manager.
The fact that he lied is unforgivable.

writing.prompt: Write five sentences, each containing a different structure: a noun clause as subject, a noun clause after a preposition, a reduced relative clause, a nominal relative clause, and a noun clause in apposition.
writing.example: What you choose matters. I'm proud of what you achieved. The boy chosen is here. Whoever tries wins. The idea that we can change is powerful.

challenge.q: Identify the function of the clause: 'My belief is that honesty pays.'
challenge.explanation: It completes the linking verb 'is' — a noun clause as complement.

challenge.q: Which sentence correctly reduces the relative clause? 'The road that leads to the village is narrow.'
options: The road leading to the village is narrow.
The road led to the village is narrow.
The road which leading to the village is narrow.
The road to lead the village is narrow.

challenge.q: Choose the correct nominal relative: '___ you say will be noted.'
challenge.explanation: 'Whatever you say' = the thing(s) that you say — a nominal relative subject.
